title: Candlestick Words Improve Intraday Volatility Forecasts Beyond HAR and GARCH
abstract: We turn each 1-minute bar into a word built from four parts: its shape, its intensity, its range-to-volume balance and its relation to the previous bar. We then ask whether these words improve 15-minute volatility forecasts beyond the standard public intraday models: HAR, HAR with signed semivariances and jumps (HAR-RS-J), multiplicative component GARCH and Realized GARCH. We call the model with the words added HAR-W. The tests use QQQ, TSLA and US small caps on data the models never saw. They were registered in advance and judged against the best benchmark chosen after the fact, on two losses (MSE of log volatility and QLIKE). The words pass 10 of 12 tests. After volatility spikes they add 1.7 to 3.7 points of out-of-sample R² and cut QLIKE by 4% to 9%. At every minute the gain is smaller but consistent: 0.5 to 1.3 points and 1.6% to 4.2%. In every model confidence set, a model with the words survives. On daily bars the words add nothing beyond HAR, so the effect is an intraday phenomenon. Against Kronos, a pre-trained foundation model for candles, the words still add to the best benchmark after spikes on QQQ and TSLA; on small caps they add to it but miss the registered R² bar by a hair (4 of 6 tests pass). The spike bar and the three bars after it carry most of the gain (+0.74 R² points on the hold-out year). The words do not predict direction.
why: Pre-registered intraday volatility test with OOS losses and strong benchmarks

title: From SEC Filings to Financial Signals: Evaluating LLMs on Stock Market Reactions and Analyst Forecasts
abstract: Form 10-Q MD&A sections combine long-form management narrative with accounting and forward-looking information. Benchmarks for financial filings commonly evaluate question answering or numerical reasoning, leaving unclear whether outputs from large language models (LLMs) align with market and analyst outcomes. We evaluate prompted, zero-shot outputs from 13 general-purpose and finance-specialized LLMs on 45,964 Form 10-Q filing events from 2001 to 2024, linking MD&A text to cross-sectional fundamental ranks, pre-filing analyst forecasts, and realized abnormal returns. The evaluation covers return ranking under five controlled information views and next-quarter EPS forecasting under direct and consensus-anchored interfaces. Relative to disclosure alone, adding cross-sectional fundamental ranks raises mean effective-date rank correlation (RankIC) by 0.0089 for effective-event-date returns and 0.0098 for following-day returns, whereas analyst-summary context provides no comparable average gain. Across the four disclosure-containing views, finance-specialized models show an effective-event-date group advantage but no statistically reliable following-day advantage, while general-purpose Qwen models produce the strongest individual return-ranking results. Under the full-information view, direct LLM forecasts average the 43.4th percentile of the analyst distribution and do not consistently beat individual analysts. Consensus anchoring raises the mean inside-range share from 41.1% to 59.5% but increases reported-EPS error.
why: LLMs on 10-Q filings vs market reactions across 45k events

title: Unbounded Losses, Unchecked Inputs: Measuring the Safeguards of LLM Options-Trading Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now place options orders at retail brokers, and developers publish open-source options agents faster than anyone has examined them. Prior security work on trading agents scored academic equities designs by whether an attacker can flip a buy-or-sell decision. We present the first measurement of the options agents that brokers and developers ship, scored by the safeguards they enforce and by the worst loss their documented order paths can reach. We screened 765 GitHub repositories, broker documentation, and the research literature and found 215 eligible repositories and 8 broker-native agent interfaces. We then scored 26 systems, including every broker interface and every open-source project with at least 20 stars, on seven robustness and eleven security safeguards with cell-level evidence. The ecosystem is new: 198 of the 215 repositories were created in 2026, and 129 (60.0%) appeared in the two weeks around one options-trading hackathon. Of the 22 systems that can place orders, 10 enforce a pre-trade limit outside the model, yet none of the 26 authenticate their text sources or cross-check market data. Of the 26, 17 can execute with no mandatory human step and 13 can reach unbounded loss, including 6 of the 8 broker interfaces. Because an attacker who writes the agent's inputs can move an order's strike, expiry, volatility, and legs while its direction stays correct, options agents need loss limits enforced at the order boundary.
why: Measures safeguards of shipped LLM options agents; practitioner-relevant risk audit

title: More Mentions, Less Information? Diagnosing Identity and Alignment in Reddit Embeddings for Volatility Forecasting
abstract: Since the 2021 GameStop short squeeze, r/WallStreetBets (WSB) has been associated with episodes of extreme volatility, and its text is increasingly used to forecast volatility. A model using only large language model (LLM) embeddings of WSB posts attains an out-of-sample $R^2$ of 0.13 for log realized variance. That number shows predictive power, but it does not reveal where the information comes from or how much the text adds beyond a firm's own volatility history. We answer these questions with a diagnostic protocol that nests embeddings on a heterogeneous autoregressive (HAR) benchmark, compares them with text-free firm-identity controls, shuffles the day-to-text pairing within firm-years to test day-specific alignment, and checks whether gains persist across periods and coverage groups. We apply the protocol to frozen LLM embeddings in a panel of 202,145 mentioned stock-days, using retrospective rolling out-of-sample tests over 2015-2022. The results indicate that most of the standalone fit reflects firm or firm-year information: on firms seen in training, a text-free firm baseline reaches $R^2 = 0.32$, shuffling preserves 89-92% of the standalone fit, and masking ticker strings reduces standalone $R^2$ to -0.005. Adding embeddings to HAR reduces equal-date MSE by 1.22% (95% CI [0.94, 1.49]). This small but statistically significant gain survives firm controls and ticker masking, but is largely eliminated by alignment shuffling. The gain is concentrated in 2015-2019 and is not distinguishable from zero in 2020-2022. Expanding coverage by 48% through off-hours and weekend posts adds stock-days with no reliable positive increment. More mentions therefore do not imply more incremental forecasting information.
why: Diagnoses where Reddit embedding volatility signal comes from; strong evaluation

title: Reliable Before Profitable: QuantHarness for Governing Financial Strategy Development with LLM Agents
abstract: LLM agents can turn natural-language financial research requests into executable and backtested strategies, but a successful run may still implement the wrong rule, use information unavailable at decision time, or obscure how repairs and candidate selection changed the strategy. Because these failures arise throughout development, final code and performance metrics alone are insufficient to establish either fidelity to the request or the validity of the development process. We therefore address the reliability of financial strategy development at the trajectory level: the system must control how intermediate outputs become downstream state and preserve the evidence needed to justify the terminal outcome. We introduce QuantHarness, a two-layer agent harness in which a finance-specific Workflow structures specification, data grounding, construction, testing, and review, while Harness Core enforces stage-specific information, action, and commitment boundaries. We also introduce FinRelBench, a benchmark that evaluates strategy-development reliability through execution success, requirement satisfaction, and runtime evidence. QuantHarness achieves the highest Task Success at 90.72\%, compared with 74.23\%--84.54\% for the comparison systems. Controlled stress tests show that its boundaries contain targeted violations, while structured run records improve evidence retrieval and support decision replay under the evaluated protocol.
why: Trajectory-level governance of LLM strategy development; look-ahead and fidelity checks.

title: Beyond Behavioral Accuracy: Evaluating Individual-Level Fidelity in LLM Investor Simulation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as user simulators, but can they faithfully reproduce an individual's behavior and decision logic over time? We investigate this question in a longitudinal paper-trading study with 80 participants. Using rolling next-day predictions, we evaluate trading activity, buy-sell structure, asset selection, and portfolio outcomes, complemented by controlled input ablations and participant-rated explanation alignment. No evaluated LLM reliably outperforms a simple recent-activity persistence baseline for predicting trade occurrence, while buy-sell structure and asset selection remain difficult to reproduce. Similar activity-level performance can also yield substantially different portfolio trajectories. Ablations show that activity predictions depend primarily on recent trades, whereas asset choices are sensitive to multiple evidence sources. Participants rate explanations as more aligned with their recurring strategies than with their decision-specific rationales. These findings reveal a gap between coarse behavioral agreement and individual-level fidelity, motivating separate evaluation of behavioral accuracy, explanation alignment, and evidence dependence in personalized user simulation.
why: LLM investor simulation fails to beat persistence baseline; strong evaluation

title: Headwind or tailwind? How banks interpret borrowers’ AI exposure
abstract: General-purpose technologies create large opportunities but make their distribution across firms difficult to assess in real time. We use banks as interpreters of the rise of generative AI by studying lender-specific probability-of-default (PD) estimates for private firms in four large euro-area economies. As public attention to AI rises after ChatGPT, banks lower assessed default risk for borrowers in highly AI-exposed industries by about 5%. The reassessment is weaker for labor-intensive firms and stronger among lenders with pre-existing industry expertise. Yet the favorable industry-level effect is accompanied by a systematic reordering within product markets: banks reassess firms with stronger pre-ChatGPT market positions less favorably relative to their competitors, compressing the risk advantage associated with market leadership. Credit allocation moves in the same direction, with market leaders experiencing relatively lower drawn and committed credit, more relationship exits, and fewer new lenders. The reordering also predicts subsequent bad-credit events beyond banks’ consensus PDs. Internal bank assessments therefore provide a forward-looking measure of how generative AI is expected to reshape competitive risk.
why: Bank PD reassessment of AI-exposed borrowers; real lender data, surprising

title: Rachev-Ratio Portfolio Optimization with TimeGAN Scenarios: Replacement versus Supplementation
abstract: This study evaluates the reliability and investment consequences of scenarios from a specified time-series generative adversarial network (TimeGAN) in Rachev-ratio portfolio allocation. Using 12 exchange-traded funds, we compare historical, replacement and hybrid policies across five training seeds with delayed execution and transaction costs. Synthetic probability mass varies independently of draw count under a fixed training protocol; optimal generator fidelity is not assumed. Generated scenarios understate volatility and tail losses and distort dependence. Limited longer-training diagnostics improve reconstruction loss without improving cross-asset correlation accuracy. Higher-mass hybrids earn larger average net returns in some configurations, but all conditional generated-versus-historical return intervals include zero at the reference block length. Full-period TimeGAN means exceed resampling controls, while direct paired return, Sharpe and realized-tail-ratio intervals include zero. Replacement raises turnover and is sensitive to the modified objective's denominator floor; changing that floor does not uniformly improve realized downside risk. Exploratory generation-error associations do not identify a causal investment-performance channel. The results illustrate financial model risk from the interaction of imperfect scenarios and a tail-sensitive allocation criterion, supporting joint evaluation of fidelity, numerical behavior and realized outcomes within the tested implementation.
why: TimeGAN scenarios in Rachev allocation; negative-leaning, costs included

title: Adversarial Post-Training of Foundation Models for High-Frequency Trading
abstract: While autoregressive foundation models trained on limit order book (LOB) data show state-of-the-art performance for market simulation, pre-training with cross-entropy neither penalizes the compounding of sampling errors over free-running rollouts nor targets desired market properties. We introduce a post-training method for LOB foundation models using a Wasserstein generative adversarial network (GAN) objective. A critic, trained online on rollouts through the true, non-differentiable matching engine, guides updates from evolution strategies over rank-4 LoRA perturbations of the pre-trained generator, under a KL trust region. For efficiency, we use EGGROLL (Evolution Guided GeneRal Optimisation via Low-rank Learning), a memory-efficient variant of evolution strategies. On a held-out panel, adversarial post-training improves LOB-Bench realism by 17.6% (WS-21) and 17.0% (Mean-$L_1$), while selection-matched random-perturbation and compute-matched continued-pre-training controls yield no improvement. Post-training is thus a necessary stage that more pre-training does not replace. Per-position divergence measurements show that it slows error accumulation over 500-message rollouts from $3.1\times$ to $2.3\times$. Adversarial post-training is also inexpensive, requiring under 50M training tokens and 12 GPU-hours per seed, three orders of magnitude below the 48B-token pre-training budget. Ablations over critic inputs, optimizers, and the population-rollout trade-off, together with an analysis of reward hacking, yield practical design guidelines for adversarial post-training.
why: Adversarial post-training of LOB foundation models; real matching-engine realism.

title: Evidence Sufficiency and Model Comparisons in MexRegQA: An Item-Level Audit of Mexican-Spanish Regulatory QA
abstract: Similarity-gated coverage does not establish that retrieved evidence contains the facts needed to answer a question. We audit Mexican-Spanish financial-regulatory QA and find that 35 of 135 covered items lack some or all load-bearing facts. On the post-hoc full-evidence slice (n=98), eleven prompt-matched models score 95-98/98 and none differs significantly from the anchor; this does not establish equivalence. Removing evidence-defective items changes the nominal significance status of 14 of 55 pairwise comparisons. On 56 zero-evidence items, accuracy spans 33.9%-89.3%. Removing evidence from the audited items under an abstention-permitting prompt reduces accuracy by 63-81 percentage points in all ten tested legs, with no recovered items. Building on sufficient-context research, we contribute MexRegQA v1.0: 192 items with provenance and evidence-status labels, frozen retrieval evidence for 191 evaluated items, predictions, judge outputs and offline checks. The audit was outcome-aware, the later model/panel sweep reused the same questions, and all reported scores and labels rely on machine evaluation without independent human validation. We propose releasing evidence-status labels alongside grounded QA benchmarks so that model comparisons can be examined separately from evidence availability.
why: Item-level audit of financial-regulatory QA evidence; strong evaluation discipline.

title: Amortized Neural Filtering for Calibrated Posteriors in Statistical Arbitrage
abstract: Statistical arbitrage trades on an estimate of the state of a residual spread, and conventional practice discards the uncertainty of that estimate. We keep the uncertainty and use it in the trading decision. A Neural Filter Estimator (NFE) is trained on simulated paths of a mean-reverting process whose innovation law is selected by testing candidates against real residuals; once trained, it returns the posterior over the latent state of every spread in a cross-section in one forward pass. Three results follow. On simulated paths with known truth, every practical estimator, ours included, falls in one narrow band of accuracy well below an estimator given full information, so the posterior gains no accuracy over a point estimate; its contribution is a correct account of its own uncertainty. On Korean equities, net of costs, the conventional point estimate forecasts about a thousand basis points per holding period more than it realizes, and the amortized methods cut that gap by a factor of roughly two to eight. Sizing positions from the posterior on the same learned factors as the end-to-end Attention Factor Model matches the Sharpe ratio of those factors under the base rule within the period's noise, at no more risk.
why: Calibrated stat-arb posteriors, net of costs on Korean equities

title: Conflicting History in Foundation Model Return Forecasts
abstract: Older observations can help a forecaster learn a predictive relationship while becoming misleading when that relationship changes. We study this tension using paired return histories that differ in older observations but share recent returns and the conditional distribution of the next return. Across five foundation-model forecasting procedures and three simulated processes, each evaluated on 1,024 independent replications, conflicting history reduces the probability of improving on zero in all 30 higher-signal comparisons. This loss of usefulness occurs despite successful signal recovery under stable conditions. A separate exploratory comparison on 56 assets finds that shortening inputs from 256 to 64 returns increases mean absolute error for every model by 1.77-4.58 basis points; neither length improves observed overall error over zero. The evidence distinguishes the ability to extract a signal from the ability to withstand conflicting history, while showing why context sensitivity alone does not justify discarding older data.
why: Shows conflicting history hurts foundation-model return forecasts; negative result

title: The Control Layer Behind Rule-Following Agents Trading Across Market Conditions
abstract: Trading discipline often fails people. Our study tested whether four AI trading agents followed their strategies and risk rules. Offering traders the evidence and an agent evaluation toolkit to separate luck from following the rules, before giving agents meaningful autonomy or capital. Our study analysed 2,627 closed positions from 12 February to 27 August 2026 across the same asset universe and execution conditions. Most positions were simulated against live prices with a 0.09% round-trip fee; 18% involved real Hyperliquid orders. Each position declared a strategy, stop and target, with a limit of five open positions per agent. The fleet finished net positive after fees. Rule adherence was high across all four agents, including the unprofitable one. Profitability tracked how often agents won relative to their break-even win rates. Institutional-style controls ran by default and contained losses through a 29% market drawdown and recovery, with documented exceptions. The discipline held for all four agents. Agents kept 97.5% of gross loss within declared stops, and typical losses closed at declared levels. Declared risk remained stable after losses and broadly stable across calm and volatile months. Twenty-three of 24 runs respected the position limit; logs identify the exception's size and duration. The same live data produced different results across assigned strategies. The trade-log tests can be rerun from the published trade snapshot; regime tests also require the published Bitcoin prices and regime labels. Section 3.5 specifies the stop-breach tolerance. These trade-level results are not account-level returns or proof of a lasting edge. Our study provides an evaluation toolkit to help traders distinguish rule-following from luck before committing capital. For anyone considering allocating capital to agents to trade, discipline should be the entry test, not the only test.
why: Trading agents rule adherence with real Hyperliquid orders

title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Market Making on Prediction-Market Order Books
abstract: A market maker provides liquidity by quoting prices to buy and sell an asset, earning the spread while managing inventory risk. We study market makers trained with multi-agent reinforcement learning on prediction markets, specifically Polymarket, whose thin order books pose distinct challenges. Three challenges underpin this research: adverse selection may cause a policy trained on real data to stop quoting; the consequences of a quote can arrive many steps after the action; and prediction-market L2 data does not identify individual orders needed for simulation. We address these challenges by reconstructing order-level LOBSTER-format data from Polymarket and training agents in JaxMARL-HFT on 417 real markets. We enrich the baseline market maker's observation space with the book and recent flow, redesign its actions and inventory controls, and propose a cooperative multi-agent decomposition into a quoter and a risk manager trained using recurrent Independent Proximal Policy Optimisation (IPPO) with RNN policies. We investigate reward shaping, particularly reward blending and post-fill markout, to mitigate credit-assignment difficulties between the agents. Our redesigned single-agent market maker quotes more frequently and incurs smaller held-out losses than the retrained JaxMARL-HFT baseline, although the contributions of jointly changed observations, actions and risk constraints are not separately identified. Decomposition alone performs poorly; careful reward design substantially improves the desk relative to the unshaped split and yields our best result. Models are evaluated on realised end-of-episode portfolio value on held-out markets. None establishes positive average portfolio value in periodic held-out evaluation, and each configuration was trained with one seed. The environment, data and protocol lay a foundation for makers that quote many linked markets at once.
why: MARL market making on reconstructed real Polymarket order books

title: Bureau Event Foundation Models on Synthetic Credit-Bureau Histories: When do Sequence Models Add to Engineered Features?
abstract: Gradient-boosted trees on engineered bureau aggregates are the standard for credit risk, while transformer sequence models pre-trained without labels are increasingly applied to financial event streams. Whether the latter add to well-engineered aggregates is hard to study openly because bureau data are confidential. We introduce SynBureau, an agent-based simulator that produces complete synthetic credit-bureau reportsconsumer data, a generic score, accounts with all standard fields and 36-month payment histories, and enquiries-with outcomes from 5 to 90 days past due, and a parameter that controls how much information lies in the order and timing of events. On these data we compare a Bureau Event Foundation Model (BEFM), pre-trained by masked event modelling, a hybrid that reads the event sequence and 101 engineered variables together, and a tuned LightGBM, with every choice made on validation data, independent holdout worlds scored once and three training seeds. The sequence model alone trailed LightGBM in every world (Δ Gini-0.060,-0.039,-0.028 for increasing temporal structure). A validationweighted blend of the hybrid with LightGBM was ahead in every world and seed (Δ Gini +0.003, +0.007, +0.004 for increasing temporal structure), with paired intervals excluding zero. Larger label-free pre-training did not help. Sequence representations add a small, consistent gain on top of engineered features rather than replacing them. All data are synthetic.
why: Synthetic bureau data benchmark; useful for credit but simulated and forgettable.

title: Reinforcement Learning Agents in Limit Order Books: Equilibrium Dynamics and Market Impact
abstract: This paper investigates the strategic behavior and market impact of deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents operating within a high-frequency continuous double auction limit order book (LOB) environment. Utilizing a multi-agent framework governed by Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), we examine how autonomous trading agents learn optimal execution, quoting, and inventory management strategies under varying degrees of market friction and order flow toxicity. Our findings indicate that RL agents naturally discover canonical market-making behaviors, widening spreads under high inventory risk and engaging in predatory order-spoofing during high-volatility regimes. Furthermore, we analyze the permanent and temporary price impact generated by agent execution policies, demonstrating that RL-driven strategies significantly minimize implementation shortfalls relative to static benchmark execution algorithms (TWAP and VWAP).
why: Simulated RL market-making agents with spoofing; no real order book validation evident.

title: Optimal Trading Filters and the Value of Predictive Signals
abstract: The value of a forecast depends on its accuracy, but also on its actionability. In trading, an investor must translate return forecasts into positions while accounting for trading costs and the lingering impact of earlier trades. We solve the stationary quadratic trading problem with transient price impact using tools from prediction theory: Wiener-Hopf factorization gives the optimal policy as the composition of a conditional forecast and an explicit causal linear filter. We recover the Gârleanu-Pedersen aim-portfolio under exponential resilience and derive fractional trading filters under power-law impact decay, requiring memory beyond finite-dimensional LQR control. At fixed positive risk penalty, signals of equal instantaneous predictive strength have equal frictionless Markowitz value. With trading costs, net attainable value is determined by the mean square of the friction-weighted conditional forecast. Under power-law impact with exposure bleeding, we find an intermediate optimal mean-reversion rate for Ornstein-Uhlenbeck signals.
why: Optimal trading filters with impact; theory, no empirical data

title: Bias correcting transaction cost models for characteristic function based estimators
abstract: Effective transaction cost is a necessary step for devising any competing financial trading strategy in the absence of quote data. Classically, Roll's model estimated the transaction cost using the first order autocovariance of the difference between daily transaction prices, while Hasbrouck's Bayesian approach used iterative posterior simulation. However, Roll's model fails when the first order autocovariance becomes positive, while Hasbrouck's estimator is computationally intensive, especially when many securities are involved. We develop empirical characteristic function methods with a first order bias correcting for spread estimation, and establish the asymptotic distribution of the corrected estimator under suitable conditions. Our numerical experiments illustrate the bias-variance tradeoff of characteristic-function methods compared to Roll's model, and their computational advantage over Hasbrouck's model.
why: Spread estimator bias correction; practical but narrow econometrics

title: Probabilistic Limit Order Book Forecasting with Conditional Diffusion Models
abstract: Modeling limit order book (LOB) dynamics is central to market forecasting and execution-strategy evaluation. While diffusion models achieve strong empirical performance, existing LOB snapshot models typically lack a learned recurrent encoder and formal statistical guarantees. We introduce LOBGrad, a conditional DDPM framework for probabilistic LOB forecasting that combines an autoregressive RNN encoder with a diffusion-based generator. In particular, we establish an excess-risk oracle inequality for the one-step DDPM noise-prediction objective under exponential mixing and regularity assumptions. We further show that, under contractive dynamics, the dependence on the conditioning-window length can be reduced to a dependence on the latent-state dimension. Experiments on BTC/USDT, GOOGL, and META show that LOBGrad improves on its encoder-free diffusion ablation across all reported queue metrics and obtains competitive results against other baselines. It also reproduces the key stylized facts of LOB microstructure, and yields reasonably calibrated queue-based predictive intervals. A stylized downstream task illustrates the potential value of the generated forecasts.
why: Diffusion LOB forecaster with theory; real order books but no costs.

title: FinHopper: A Progressive Multi-Hop Benchmark for Complex Financial Agents with Step-wise Evaluation
abstract: Financial agents are expected to answer factual investment queries through open search, but financial multi-hop retrieval differs from general multi-hop QA in a crucial way: each intermediate answer is an exact typed constraint, such as an entity, date, event, or numerical indicator, that determines the next query. This strict answer-conditioned dependency makes small intermediate errors cascade into plausible but wrong search trajectories. We introduce FinHopper, a benchmark for complex financial agents with controlled reasoning depth from 1 to 6 hops, covering stocks, funds, and macroeconomic facts, with gold intermediate answers for process-level evaluation. To construct FinHopper at scale, we design a state-transition-based synthesis framework that composes verified atomic financial QA patterns into dependency-preserving chains, followed by targeted in-synthesis verification, model-ensemble checking, and public-search validation by financial experts. Experiments with 20 LLM-agent configurations show that public search tools are necessary but insufficient: performance drops sharply as hop depth increases, the best model remains far below human experts, and process-aware scoring reveals partial reasoning progress hidden by final-answer-only evaluation. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/justajustin/FinHopper/.
why: Multi-hop financial agent benchmark with step-wise evaluation; benchmark only.

title: Regime-Aware Interpretable Ranking for Sector Rotation
abstract: Sector rotation is a common decision in benchmark-relative portfolio management, where portfolio managers rank sectors for overweight and underweight positions. We formulate this task as ranking sector actions by expected future risk-adjusted active performance, measured with forward sector-benchmark Sharpe ratios. Such rankings should preserve temporal information, express model outputs through economically familiar signal characteristics, account for changes in signal relevance across macroeconomic environments, and capture dependencies among sectors. We propose RegimeRank, an interpretable sector-ranking model that represents fundamental and technical signals through expert-defined temporal characteristics, conditions them on learned macro factors via cross-attention, and models cross-sector dependencies through self-attention. Expected-gradient attributions identify the contributions of individual signal-transformation pairs, while macroeconomic and cross-sector attention maps provide diagnostics of the learned conditioning and relational structure. We evaluate RegimeRank on weekly S&P 500 data from 2002 to 2024 under combinatorial purged cross-validation, where it outperforms representative ranking and machine-learning baselines across multiple ranking metrics. Ablation studies support the contributions of latent macro states, regime conditioning, and cross-sector modelling, while attribution and attention analyses illustrate the temporal characteristics, macro states, and sector relationships underlying its rankings.
why: Interpretable sector ranking with attributions; reasonable but no clear edge.

title: A Behavioural Twin as the Engine of an On-device Language-model Credit Analyst: Evidence from a Synthetic Credit-bureau World with Known Causes of Default
abstract: Language models are being tried as credit analysts, but sending applicants' credit histories to cloud models is often not acceptable, and small models that run on a lender's own hardware are not risk models. We propose a division of labour in which a generative bureau-event transformer-the FBFM twin-simulates many futures of the applicant's own credit history and returns a risk estimate and counterfactual drivers, and an in-house small language model reads the bureau report with this twin report and returns a decision and reason; both run on one machine. Because the true reason for a default is unknown in real data, we evaluate in SynBureau, a fully synthetic agent-based credit-bureau world whose simulator records each borrower's hidden mechanism. The twin's counterfactual drivers matched the true mechanism for credit-search and past-delinquency defaulters 1.8 and 3.5 times more often than for other borrowers, and the twin did not claim to foresee shocks after the application. A local 8B model (4-bit) alone ranked defaulters poorly (Gini 0.066), approved every applicant and called nearly every file clean; with the twin report its Gini rose to 0.201 (Δ +0.134, 95% CI [+0.016, +0.250]). With a calibrated report and a stated risk appetite, its decisions followed the twin and its stated reasons matched the true mechanism several times more often than chance. A tuned gradient-boosting model still ranked best. Grounding a local language model in a simulator of the borrower's own futures makes it a usable, private credit analyst. All data are synthetic.
why: On-device LLM credit analyst on synthetic bureau data; narrow

title: Estimating Decision Rules from Large Language Model Agents: An Application to Bank Balance-Sheet Management
abstract: This paper examines whether decisions generated by large language model (LLM) agents can be represented by simple equations in an agent-based model of bank balance-sheet management. In a monthly leader-follower model, a stylised, predominantly deposit-funded euro-area bank chooses deposit rates, lending margins and the composition of bond reinvestment, while depositors and borrowers respond to these decisions and to economic conditions. The initial balance sheet is calibrated to selected indicators from regulatory disclosures. We estimate equation-based approximations of LLM-generated decisions and evaluate them against simulations not used in estimation. Across ten out-of-sample bank-year simulations, the final specification reproduces annual return on equity (ROE) within 0.31 percentage points and meets all fit criteria in seven; none of the deposit-run scenarios meets all criteria. In eighteen simulations with a second LLM family, the ROE difference does not exceed 0.71 percentage points, but only six meet all criteria. Against a market-pricing rule, the original optimisation model, and regression and nearest-neighbour approximations estimated on the same data, the final specification meets all criteria in more years and tracks liquidity most closely in deposit-run years. Instructions without behavioural guidance show that withdrawal magnitudes and fixed-rate borrowers' price sensitivity depend materially on the instructions supplied; with customer equations estimated under neutral instructions, a two-month withdrawal episode no longer becomes self-sustaining. The results demonstrate a procedure for approximating and evaluating LLM-generated decisions within a defined simulation environment; they do not establish that these responses represent the behaviour of bank managers or customers. AI-use disclosure: Large language models are used as simulated decision-making agents in this study. Separately, Claude assisted with simulation-code development, bibliographic checking and editorial consistency, and ChatGPT assisted with manuscript editing and condensation. The author is responsible for the research design, analyses, interpretation and final text.
why: Equation approximations of LLM bank decisions; ABM, no market data

title: Constraint-Aware Adversarial Defense for Financial Fraud Detection Models in Cloud-Native Banking Architectures
abstract: Financial fraud detection models deployed in cloud-native banking architectures face a growing but underexamined threat: adversarial attacks that respect the operational constraints of real transaction systems. Unlike laboratory adversarial machine learning, where perturbations are bounded only by generic norm constraints, attackers targeting banking fraud detectors operate under strict domain rules-transaction amounts must fall within plausible ranges, merchant categories must remain valid, and timestamps must follow realistic sequences. Recent evidence indicates that under such constraint-aware attacks, the detection performance of widely deployed gradient-boosted fraud models can collapse dramatically, yet existing defense methods are almost exclusively evaluated under unconstrained perturbation assumptions, leaving a critical gap between research benchmarks and production reality. This study addresses that gap by (1) formalizing a threat model for constraint-aware adversarial attacks against financial fraud detection, (2) constructing a benchmark of semantically valid adversarial transaction samples derived from realistic banking feature constraints, and (3) proposing and evaluating a constraint-aware defense framework that combines adversarial training with inference-time semantic consistency checking, designed for deployment in cloudnative environments where latency and throughput budgets are tight. Experiments will compare the proposed framework against standard adversarial training and feature-squeezing baselines across gradient-boosted and deep learning detectors, measuring robustness (F1 under attack), clean performance, and inference overhead. The study contributes a deployment-oriented robustness evaluation methodology and practical defense guidance for financial institutions adopting AI-driven fraud detection in emerging and developed digital banking markets.
why: Constraint-aware fraud defense; applied but incremental benchmark work

title: The impact of Generative AI on Venture Capital Investment Decisions
abstract: This study examines how the global release of a widely accessible and highly impactful generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tool influenced Venture Capital (VC) investors’ allocation decisions. We argue that the release of ChatGPT in late 2022 reduced the informational opacity surrounding generative AI, which had historically made AI-related ventures particularly difficult for generalist investors to evaluate, thereby triggering a reallocation of capital toward AI ventures relative to non-AI firms. Leveraging a global dataset of VC transactions from 2019 to 2024, we implement a difference-in-differences strategy and show that ChatGPT’s release significantly increased AI-related investments, both in deal volume and transaction count. The effect is strongest for early-stage ventures, where informational frictions were previously most binding, consistent with the information asymmetry mechanism. It is further amplified in countries with higher AI preparedness and digital adoption and in technologically intensive industries. Moreover, AI-related VC activity exhibits no systematic pre-treatment trends, suggesting that even specialized investors required a tangible public signal before reallocating capital at scale. These results provide the first causal evidence that a generative AI breakthrough reshapes the allocation of entrepreneurial finance and the first direct test of whether VCs anticipate or react to a major technological megatrend.
why: DiD on ChatGPT and VC allocation; sound but descriptive

title: How Is the AI Build-Out Financed? Internal Funds, Leases, and Depreciation Compared with the Dot-Com Boom
abstract: We compare the financing of the AI infrastructure build-out with that of the dot-com build-out, using one selection rule and one cash measure: capital expenditure minus operating cash flow, scaled by sales (the gap). Through 2025 the ten largest capital spenders in the build-out industries generated more operating cash than they spent on capital, in aggregate; their dot-com counterparts did not by 2001. The aggregate hides dispersion. In the four quarters to mid-2026 Oracle’s capital spending was 1.74 times its operating cash flow and Amazon’s slightly exceeded it. The five hyperscalers borrowed $234 billion net and added $224 billion to cash. Their $1.09 trillion of leases not yet begun would raise their gap from -6.8% to about -3% of sales once payments start; treated as purchases spread over three to ten years, the gap would be between -3.6% and +6.8%. Faster server depreciation would lower 2025 operating income by a few percent. In daily data for 1996–2025, the gap does not reliably condition tail co-movement between the builders and the rest of the market.
why: Cash-flow financing analysis of AI capex versus dot-com; useful context, no method.

title: Conditional Weight of Evidence for Gradient-Boosted Credit Models: Estimation, Additivity and Its Relation to Adverse Action Reasons
abstract: Traditional weight of evidence assigns a credit characteristic a value based on its association with default across a population. Credit analysis also requires an assessment of that characteristic in the context of an individual applicant's record. We study conditional weight of evidence for this purpose. It measures the change in default log odds from observing a characteristic after the remaining credit information is known. Its sign identifies whether the characteristic adds adverse or favorable information for that applicant, and its magnitude measures the strength of that information. The same characteristic value can therefore receive different assessments for applicants with different payment histories or other credit attributes. We develop estimators using gradient-boosted trees and evaluate their accuracy in a bureau-style simulation. Regressions of the full model's predicted probabilities recover conditional evidence more accurately than separate models fitted to default outcomes, provided the full model is accurate. They also recover a deliberately constructed file-age effect whose direction varies with utilization and is often missed by marginal weight of evidence. Local class-frequency estimates improve on marginal weight of evidence but remain inaccurate for some weak effects. An application to FICO HELOC data illustrates estimation when the population evidence is unknown. Conditional weight of evidence provides an applicant-specific interpretation of the information in a credit characteristic; its population summary, a conditional information value, splits the joint information in the record across blocks when averaged over orderings. Neither is an adverse action reason, which explains the fitted score difference between the applicant and chosen passing records.
why: Conditional WoE for GBM credit; useful method, no market data

title: Arbitrage-Free Implied Volatility Surface Reconstruction via Additive Martingales
abstract: This work focuses on reconstructing a continuous implied volatility (IV) surface from a small number of option quotes, a fundamental task for option pricing and risk management. We propose Additive Martingale (AddMart), a few-shot IV surface reconstruction framework that satisfies static no-arbitrage conditions by construction. Rather than predicting IVs directly, AddMart maps sparse quotes to non-negative increment densities of an exponential additive martingale, from which valid risk-neutral marginals and IVs are recovered. By incorporating the no-arbitrage structure directly into its architecture, rather than enforcing it through regularization in the learning objective, AddMart produces IV surfaces that satisfy static no-arbitrage conditions throughout the domain. Extensive experiments on ten real-option datasets demonstrate that AddMart achieves competitive reconstruction accuracy with no material static arbitrage violations, while directly enabling the estimation of VaR, CVaR, and crash probabilities.
why: No-arbitrage IV surface reconstruction; solid but not AI-finance

title: Trading Literature Atlas For Semi-automated Systematic Trading
abstract: Research that matters for systematic trading is scattered across communities that rarely read one another. Time-series classification, deep learning, empirical finance, market microstructure, derivatives, rough-path mathematics, statistics, decision theory, language models and practitioner writing each study objects that a trading desk needs, such as regimes, labels, liquidity, crosssections and search over signals, but they name them differently and often study them in isolation. This manuscript is a contribution in bridge-building. It builds a common vocabulary so that traders can find better alphas and so that mathematicians and machine-learning researchers can see where their skills apply in a hard, noisy, adversarial domain. The setting throughout is a semi-automated systematic fund. The evidence base is a Zotero collection of 1065 papers. An automated classification of titles and abstracts assigned each paper to one of 11 research silos, to one or more of 11 stages of a fund's pipeline, and to concept tags. Fourteen topical chapters, one per cluster of the collection, review the papers on their own terms and close with bridge notes that translate jargon between silos. Desk notes turn ideas into inputs, outputs and failure modes for a trading desk. A shared vocabulary, a set of cross-silo bridges, a blueprint of the fund and a list of open gaps tie the chapters together. The reader gets a map of the literature indexed by the stages of a real pipeline, a glossary that translates between communities, a set of concrete cross-silo proposals, and an honest account of what the method can and cannot claim. Silo and stage labels rest on abstracts, not full texts, and they are produced by an automated classifier. Synthesis and proposals are ours, not the cited authors'.
why: Bibliography and vocabulary atlas for trading research; no results

title: Credit Support, Financing Expansion, and Risk Allocation in AI Infrastructure
abstract: Credit support shapes both the financing of AI infrastructure and the distribution of its downside exposure. We combine a 30-project powered-land inventory, a purposive register of 15 financing instruments across four parent groups, executed contracts and regulatory orders with a model of financing choice. Three results follow. First, support expands debt capacity under a binding expected-loss-rate constraint. When costly external equity induces use of that capacity, absolute expected lender losses increase; partial use can combine a lower loss rate with a larger monetary loss. This mechanism extends to risk budgets that rise with exposure, while a fixed monetary budget holds expected loss constant. CoreWeave's delayed-draw term-loan principal rises USD 3.972 billion in H1 2026, and Applied Digital replaces a USD 300 million bridge with USD 1.590 billion of project notes. Second, payment priority, customer acceptance, enforcement timing and power-service conditions allocate shortfalls and financial flexibility across equipment, campuses and electricity investment. Third, common support providers increase portfolio covariance at unchanged marginal credit quality. In an exact illustrative experiment, concentration raises 99 percent expected shortfall by 58.9 percent. A heterogeneous-claim extension identifies each provider's conditional loss exposure as the relevant concentration weight. Credit support is a financial production input and a contingent allocation rule. Financial-stability assessment must connect funded amounts, contractual activation states and the balance sheets supplying protection.
why: AI infrastructure credit support analysis; case-based, no transferable method

title: Geopolitical Risk, Trade War Uncertainty, and Environmental Shocks: Regime Switching Volatility and Dynamic Spillovers in Global Financial and Commodity Markets
abstract: This study examines how geopolitical risk, trade war uncertainty, and climate policy uncertainty, used here as a proxy for environmental shocks, relate to the volatility and cross market dependence of United States equities and crude oil, using monthly data from January 1990 to December 2024. We combine a Markov switching GARCH framework augmented with exogenous shock indices, a dynamic conditional correlation model, and a generalized forecast error variance decomposition, and we add a long short term memory network as a predictability check. The baseline specification identifies two weakly separated volatility states for the S&P 500 and a single state for oil. In the extended specification, the response of equity volatility to all three shocks is larger in the crisis state, with climate policy uncertainty carrying the largest coefficient, whereas the mean response of equity returns to trade war uncertainty changes from positive in the stable state to negative in the crisis state. The conditional correlation between equity and oil returns averages 0.058 and peaks at 0.231 around 2020, and equities are net transmitters of spillovers to oil, at 2.60 percentage points, with the rolling spillover index rising during the Global Financial Crisis and the pandemic. The neural network yields negative out of sample R squared values, which is consistent with weak return predictability. The findings support regime aware hedging and macroprudential monitoring, subject to the estimation caveats discussed in the paper.
why: Markov-switching volatility on macro shocks; monthly, US-only

title: Documenting And Checking Calculation Logic And Data Meaning When A Feed Or Vendor Interface Is Replaced: A Template For Long-Lived Investment-Operations Systems
abstract: When an upstream market, trading or vendor feed is replaced, acceptance testing of the long-lived systems that consume it is often written from the replacement source's specification. That specification does not establish what the existing system did with the prior source, which conventions its fields carried, or which results must survive where the new source has no equivalent. Three failures can follow without a failed load: a field keeps its name but changes its meaning; a process cannot consume the new input; and a function the replacement cannot perform is dropped because it is 'not in the new source'. This paper describes a written, ordered documentation-and-checking template for one system class, long-lived investment-operations systems, and one scenario: the replacement of a feed or vendor interface while the existing system remains the calculation and reporting engine. The template uses the existing system's documented and observed logic and meaning as the reference; records field meaning as conventions (valuation basis, time basis, composition, identifier and vintage, unit and precision); requires meaning breaks and unexplained movements to be named before acceptance; records the reasons for leaving functions on the existing system; and keeps these records after go-live for the next change. In a synthetic worked example, a group-return movement debated as market movement is traced to a change of price basis, and a function the replacement cannot perform stays on the existing system with a recorded reason. The template orders established cutover practices, including field mapping, parallel running, reconciliation and characterisation testing. It does not claim that any institution has adopted it or that supervisory guidance requires it. It does not validate the original business logic, cannot check behaviour that cannot be documented or observed, and has costs that an operation may judge not worth bearing. AI disclosure: An AI assistant (Claude, developed by Anthropic) was used in preparing this paper to restructure and expand the author's earlier draft, to draft the practice-context section and the expanded worked example, and to check citations against their primary sources. The method, its conventions and its conclusions come from the author's professional work. The author reviewed and edited all content and is fully responsible for it.
why: Feed-replacement documentation template; operational, not empirical research

title: Information Versus Enforcement Against Greenwashing: Pre-Registered Experiments in a Multi-Agent Artificial Market
abstract: Regulators can fight greenwashing by making inflated disclosures easier to see through or by fining them when audits detect them. We compare the two in an agent-based artificial market where 1,000 investors trade the shares of 200 firms. Impact investors value reported ESG scores, and investors switch types by imitation. Every period each firm chooses between costly real improvement, cheap inflation of its report that audits may detect, and doing nothing; a regulator sets transparency, audits and fines. The market is initialised on CSI 300 constituents, investor taste is calibrated to an ESG cost-of-capital slope of about 28 basis points per standard deviation, and the baseline fine is China's statutory maximum of CNY 10 million per case. In a pre-registered experiment of 59 scenarios with 30 paired seeds each: (i) policies work only through investor preference, without which firms neither improve nor inflate; (ii) raising transparency from 0.1 to 0.6 raises the true ESG level more than quadrupling the fine, and both beat the baseline, both without natural decay of the true level and at 0.2 standard deviations (SD) per year; the effect of transparency against the baseline is +0.04 and +0.33 SD at these two uncalibrated rates; (iii) fixed fines lose deterrence quickly because inflation added to an undetected case is not fined again, and they leave large firms, for which CNY 10 million is negligible, inflating in 66% of their decisions. Exploratory supplements designed after these results keep the ordering at three intermediate decay rates, when true levels revert to the mean, when every false report is fined, and when washing costs differ across firms. But the size of the information advantage depends on two assumptions. Under mean reversion at rates bounded by a rating panel, transparency beats the quadrupled fine by only +0.003 to +0.006 SD, because improvements fade while inflation persists. With a fine for every false report, the gap shrinks from +0.205 to +0.058 SD, and the plateau in fine deterrence disappears. With firm-specific washing costs, greenwashing declines gradually with transparency instead of stopping at a threshold. Market feedback strengthens the fixed-fine effect by about 11% and has no identifiable net effect on transparency. A tabular Q-learner trained on realised accounts did not reach a usable policy. A second pre-registered experiment holds the expected number of audits fixed. Auditing in proportion to market value or after jumps in reported scores does worse than random audits when firms know the rule (-0.19 and -0.14 SD): value targeting moves greenwashing from large to small firms, and firms keep new inflation below the jump threshold. With the rule hidden, neither differs from random audits. All results are conditional on the model. AI disclosure: The simulation code, the analysis scripts and drafts of this paper were written with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic), an AI model, used through Claude Code. The author directed the research, reviewed all AI-assisted output and is responsible for the content.
why: Agent-based greenwashing simulation; policy-focused, weak transfer to practice.

title: FinLoop: A Weight-Shared Looping Transformer with Adaptive Halting for Financial Signal Prediction
abstract: Deep forecasters for stock returns typically stack many task‐specific layers, which encourages overfitting on the small effective sample of financial regimes, while spending computation uniformly on calm and turbulent markets alike. We propose FinLoop, a compact looping transformer for financial signal prediction that iteratively refines a shared latent representation of recent price history. A single pre‐norm attention block is executed K times with input injection, positional re‐injection, per‐loop embeddings, and gated per‐loop LayerScale, which lifts the expressiveness ceiling of plain weight sharing while keeping early iterations nearly identity to resist oversmoothing on noisy financial data. Each loop emits an intermediate forecast, and an adaptive‐halting unit in the spirit of adaptive computation time weighs these forecasts into a coarse‐to‐fine ensemble and enables per‐sample early exit at inference. A rank‐aware objective couples magnitude calibration with pairwise ordering supervision, per‐loop deep supervision, and an expected‐depth penalty. On a transparent CSI‐300 protocol with 300 stocks (2016 to 2020), four market regimes, eight deep baselines, and a top‐k portfolio simulation, FinLoop attains the best information coefficients, Sharpe ratio, and shallowest maximum drawdown. On a NASDAQ‐100 corpus built from the identical protocol, whose test window is dominated by extreme regimes, FinLoop again attains the best information and rank coefficients.
why: Looping transformer price forecaster; no costs or clear baseline

title: LangGraph-Orchestrated Stateful Multi-Agent Framework for Personalized Investment Advisory System Using Hybrid Forecasting and LLM Explainability
abstract: Effective investment management is currently hindered by the huge disconnect between global market intelligence and personal fiscal reality. Traditional methodologies and foundational frameworks focus primarily on market-centric analysis but remain context blind to personal liquidity, lack long-term memory, and fail to integrate real-time news. The paper proposes a novel Multi-Agent Financial Intelligence System using end-to-end personalized investment advisory with the help of Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL) and Large Language Model (LLM) techniques, designed to process personal bank statements and market data to derive data-driven Buy, Hold, Sell recommendations. A Hybrid Categorizer using Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) vectorization, a Random Forest Classifier and a LLM fallback intelligently parses and classifies bank transactions, calculating the user's investable surplus. A 10-model is run over 5 years of stock data with technical indicators such as Relative Strength Index (RSI), Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD), and Wavelet-denoised closing prices. Three Deep Learning architectures (Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) and Bidirectional LSTM) and five ML algorithms (Random Forest, XGBoost, AdaBoost, Decision Tree and Linear Regression), Auto-Regressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), and a Hybrid Model combining the top three performers are evaluated using Mean Squared Error(MSE), Mean Absolute Error(MAE), R-squared (R²). FinBERT sentiment analysis incorporates prevailing market sentiment. A user-defined risk profile stored via Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) determines Low, Medium and High risk tolerances. The pipeline is coordinated through LangGraph for stateful, sequential agent execution, with a final Gemini LLM explainability agent producing human-readable recommendations.
why: Multi-agent advisory system; no rigorous out-of-sample evaluation visible

title: Learning volatility-adaptive forgetting via GARCH-modulated LSTM for stock price forecasting
abstract: Stock price forecasting is hindered by the heteroscedastic nature of financial time series, in which turbulent and tranquil regimes alternate. Although the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network is widely used for this task, its gates are oblivious to such volatility variation, so memory retention remains fixed regardless of market conditions. A common remedy is to supply volatility estimates as an additional input feature, yet this leaves the internal memory dynamics untouched. Instead, volatility can serve as a direct regulatory signal over the gate activation itself. This paper presents the Gsigmoid-LSTM model, which embeds Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity (GARCH(1,1))-derived volatility estimates into the LSTM forgetting gate through the Gsigmoid activation function, a volatility-adaptive variant of the sigmoid that combines a volatility adjustment factor with slope regulation via a learnable parameter. The model thereby automatically prioritizes recent information during turbulent periods while preserving long-term dependencies in stable markets. In the engineering application of daily stock price forecasting, extensive experiments, including activation function comparisons, baseline evaluations, and ablation studies, demonstrate that this structural gating modification effectively improves forecasting accuracy and robustness. The proposed model significantly outperforms a feature-level fusion baseline carrying the same volatility signal on all five datasets, as confirmed by Diebold-Mariano tests with all p<0.01, attains the best average rank of 1.00 in the Friedman test across nine models, and achieves the lowest MSE and MAE on all five datasets.
why: GARCH-gated LSTM price forecaster; incremental architecture tweak

title: Dynamic Programming for Value-at-risk Markov Decision Processes in Continuous Spaces
abstract: Value-at-Risk (VaR) is a widely adopted quantile-based risk measure in practice, yet incorporating VaR objectives into Markov decision processes (VaR MDPs) remains a longstanding challenge. Recent work has derived dynamic programming equations for VaR MDPs in finite state and action spaces but left the case of more general spaces unresolved. This paper establishes, for the first time, the validity of these equations in continuous spaces, for both finite- and infinite-horizon settings. Such cases naturally arise in many real-world dynamic decision-making problems. As an application, we study an optimal execution problem with a VaR objective and demonstrate that our framework enables the characterization of optimal dynamic strategies, resolving an open question in the field.
why: Dynamic programming for VaR MDPs; theory with one application

title: World Models, Trees and Foundation Models for Retail Forecasting: Evidence from Four Public Data Sets
abstract: A retailer makes different decisions at different grains of the product, store and time hierarchy: store orders for an item in a store, supplier funding for an item across stores, category performance by store, and the financial plan for the chain. Which forecasting model to use depends on the grain. This paper compares models at each grain on four public data sets (M5, six Dominick's categories, Breakfast at the Frat, and Corporación Favorita, the last kept out of all development), over rolling forecast origins with paired tests and model confidence sets. It covers price and promotion through the plan inputs these data record, not product, assortment or place. The models are a world model that carries each item's state forward under the price and promotion plan, the same network without that state, LightGBM, the Temporal Fusion Transformer, TimesFM, Chronos-Bolt, Timestral, seasonal naive, and an equal-weight average of the world model, LightGBM and TimesFM given the plan. The answer changed with the grain. For an item by store and an item across stores, the average had the lowest error on seven and eight of nine data sets, and the 90% confidence set held a median of 1 and 2 models. For a category by store, a category and the chain total, the lowest-error model differed between data sets and a median of 4 of nine models were not separated by the four to six windows available. For category-by-store planning cost, the average or LightGBM was lowest on seven of eight data sets, and the world model was lowest only on M5; it was behind LightGBM item by store on six of eight. Every trained model used the plan, and on the weekly promotion-driven data pretrained models were less accurate without it. These results hold for these data sets; a forecast solved across all four Ps, or a retailer's own data, may give different results. Every model, test and change that lost is reported.
why: Retail forecasting model comparison; not finance-core

title: Topological Compression of Prediction Market Belief States for Event Forecasting
abstract: Topological Data Analysis (TDA) and Persistent Homology (PH) have been utilized in numerous fields$-$from protein modeling to financial analysis$-$to understand the underlying structure of data. In this paper, we incorporate TDA and PH into forecasting models over a prediction market universe to determine whether the belief state of such markets forms an underlying structure whose shape can provide predictive insight. We conclude that single-parameter PH is able to improve predictive ability and calibrated accuracy of linear forecasting models, while two-parameter multipersistence produces similar benefits for nonlinear models.
why: Persistent homology on prediction markets; weak evidence

title: AuDQ: Auditable Data Quality through Agentic Rule Discovery
abstract: High-stakes tabular pipelines rely on scattered, static quality checks that are hard to evolve and audit against policy intent. Regulated domains particularly suffer as the LLM-era automation raises expectations for traceability and accountability. We propose a vision for an ontology-grounded, repository-native data quality layer in which rules are first-class artifacts: versioned, provenance-linked to governance texts, and re-playable through immutable execution traces. As a first step toward validating this vision, we present a concrete implementation of its agentic rule-discovery core with two rule acquisition modes (Full-Agentic and Guided) and a human-in-the-loop (HITL) review interface. We define an evaluation framework and run experiments addressing whether our fully autonomous, divide-and-conquer agentic rule discovery produces rules of the same quality and diversity as those specified by a human expert, reporting preliminary results on two real world industry datasets in the finance and retail domains.
why: Agentic data-quality rule discovery; not finance-specific

title: FinSafeGuard: A Quality-Driven Synthetic Dataset for Financial AI Safety
abstract: Generating high-quality synthetic datasets at scale remains a fundamental challenge for training specialized AI systems in data-scarce domains. We present a comprehensive methodology that produces 14.3 million quality-filtered synthetic training examples from a structured taxonomy of 632,000 scenario specifications. Our four-stage pipeline ad- dresses critical challenges in synthetic data quality, diversity, and realism through: (1) systematic pre-generation research establishing optimal generation parameters via diminishing returns analysis, (2) conditional auto evolution mechanisms that remediate low-diversity batches during generation, (3) a two-layer semantic deduplication architecture combining lexical and embedding-based methods, and (4) LLM-as-Judge quality evaluation filtering samples based on behavioral correctness and tuple fidelity. Empirical analysis across three domains (Banking, Insurance, Financial Services) demonstrates domain-specific deduplication patterns ranging from 9.9% to 40.6%, with output generation modes exhibiting highest redundancy. Our batch size optimization reveals mode-specific diversity saturation thresholds, enabling principled allocation strategies. The complete pipeline reduces 26.4M raw samples to 14.3M high-confidence examples through merge (20.9% reduction), semantic deduplication (18.7% reduction), and quality-based filtering (15.9% reduction), providing a reproducible framework for domain-specific synthetic data generation with rigorous quality control.
why: Synthetic safety dataset at scale; quantity over validated financial insight.

title: Balancing Flexibility and Regulatory Risk: AI-assisted Strategies for Non-GAAP Disclosures in Competitive Markets
abstract: Purpose: This paper develops an optimal control model to analyze how firms optimize their non-GAAP disclosure strategies in competitive markets while managing regulatory risks, and examines how artificial intelligence capabilities in regulatory navigation and operational efficiency influence these optimal disclosure decisions. Design/methodology/approach: The study employs an open-loop optimal control framework with a differential-game payoff structure, using a Hamiltonian formulation and Pontryagin's Maximum Principle to derive closed-form optimal disclosure strategies. Findings: The research reveals that optimal disclosure strategies emerge from balancing the valuation benefits of disclosure flexibility against regulatory risk. AI capabilities affect firm strategy through two channels-(1) reduced regulatory sensitivity enables firms to sustain higher equilibrium flexibility levels, and (2) reduced adjustment costs accelerate convergence to target equilibrium flexibility. Comparative statics analysis identifies how competitive intensity, AI capabilities, and firm characteristics influence equilibrium disclosure choices. Originality: This paper presents the first analytical model of non-GAAP disclosure strategy that explicitly distinguishes between AI-enhanced regulatory navigation and operational efficiency, yielding closed-form solutions that facilitate rigorous comparative statics and generate testable empirical predictions. Research limitations/implications: The model employs an open-loop formulation and is limited to a two-firm setting. It assumes constant model parameters over the planning horizon and therefore does not capture time-varying market conditions or strategic feedback between firms. Practical implications: The framework provides corporate managers with analytical insights into how investments in AI-enhanced regulatory navigation and operational efficiency influence optimal disclosure strategies. It also provides regulators with a theoretical basis for understanding how AI capabilities moderate the marginal relationship between disclosure flexibility and regulatory intervention.
why: Theoretical optimal control on disclosure; AI is framing

title: Explainable Bidirectional LSTM with Bayesian Optimization for Stock Price Prediction on the Casablanca Stock Exchange: A SHAP and LIME Analysis
abstract: The stock price prediction task in the relatively under-researched arena of emerging African financial markets is especially noteworthy. In that regard, the Casablanca Stock Exchange (CSE), the leading exchange in Morocco included within the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, provides an interesting context for the forecasting task, characterized by serial correlations of lagged prices exceeding 0.99, established behavioral biases on the part of investors, and distinct sectoral responses to geopolitical events from 2022 to 2024. This paper proposes an explainable Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) network with per-stock Bayesian hyperparameter optimization via Optuna, applied to next-day closing price prediction for five CSE stocks — Maroc Telecom (IAM), Bank of Africa (BOA), Banque Centrale Populaire (BCP), Auto Hall, and STR — over a ten-year period spanning May 2016 to May 2026. A geopolitical resilience stock selection criterion explicitly excludes commodity-sensitive sectors whose price dynamics require external sentiment modeling, thereby isolating the intrinsic predictive capacity of technically-driven sequential architectures. Fourteen technical indicators spanning trend, momentum, volatility, and volume dimensions constitute the feature space. The proposed Bi-LSTM achieves a mean R² of 0.9210 on normalized predictions and a mean MAPE of 2.97% on real MAD prices, outperforming the one-directional LSTM on four of five stocks. To our knowledge, this is the first study to apply combined SHAP and LIME explainability to individual stock price prediction on the CSE. According to SHAP attribution, SMA_20 is the main predictor variable (|SHAP| = 0.1404), whereas EMA_12 represents the key trend follower indicator (|SHAP| = 0.0679). This study adds value to the body of research in deep learning in the African emerging stock markets context, providing useful insights into the functioning of the Moroccan capital market environment.
why: Single-exchange price predictor; no costs or transferable method

title: Applications of AI in Financial Research
abstract: The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning, deep learning, and large language models, is significantly transforming research activities in the field of finance. AI not only enhances data analysis and forecasting but also supports multiple stages of the research process, including literature review, data collection and processing, model development, empirical analysis, and interpretation of research findings. However, comprehensive review studies examining the role of AI throughout the entire financial research process remain limited. This paper synthesizes and analyzes representative studies to provide a comprehensive overview of the role of AI in finance research, focusing on the research process, major application areas, opportunities, challenges, and future research directions. The findings indicate that AI enhances research productivity, expands data utilization capabilities, and improves analytical performance in areas such as financial market forecasting, risk management, corporate finance, and sustainable finance. Nevertheless, the adoption of AI also raises important concerns regarding reliability, interpretability, data bias, and research ethics. The paper concludes that AI should be viewed as a research support tool rather than a replacement for researchers, emphasizing the importance of combining AI capabilities with human critical thinking to improve the quality, transparency, and credibility of finance research.
why: Review of AI in financial research; no new method

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Microfinance Digital Credit Risk Management
abstract: Contents and Reading Guide This working paper is organised into research foundations, Cambodian market evidence, model design, practical case diagnoses, implementation and governance, followed by declarations and SSRN submission materials. The headings and page sequence are intentionally structured for a forty-page manuscript. Evidence tags: Official evidence refers to regulator or multilateral statistics; literature synthesis refers to conclusions derived from published research; hypothetical cases are teaching illustrations; proposed frameworks are author research propositions requiring field validation. Operational interpretation. In operational terms, the design must identify the exact decision that changes, the staff member accountable for it, the data needed at the time, and the control that can stop or reverse an unsafe result. Documentation should connect the credit policy to model inputs, decision outputs and customer communications. Measurement considerations. Evidence should be evaluated against a predefined baseline. Relevant indicators include default at a fixed horizon, probability calibration, approval distribution, turnaround time, customer complaint incidence, override frequency and stability across regions. Results should report uncertainty and should not confuse correlation with causation. Cambodian applicability. Implementation in Cambodia requires attention to rural cash-flow seasonality, mixed formal and informal earnings, language accessibility, inconsistent connectivity and varied digital footprints. A borrower who lacks digital records is not necessarily a poor credit risk, and missing information must not automatically translate into punitive pricing. Research status: this discussion synthesizes published evidence and proposes a practical research framework; it is not a report of verified field intervention outcomes.
why: Cambodian microfinance working paper; descriptive, single-market

title: The Titanic Was Compliant: AI, Humanity And The Future Of Banking AI, Resilience And Systemic Risk In Banking Across The United States, The European Union And China
abstract: AI rules for banks are arriving unevenly in the United States, the European Union and China, and, like most financial regulation, they follow the last crisis. This paper argues that compliance is only the floor. The board's real task is to understand where AI creates material exposure and whether the bank can withstand failure. The sharpest risks are systemic: many banks relying on the same models and providers, and deposit runs that move faster than liquidity plans assume. We propose a Global AI Governance Floor built on six principles, and a 90-day agenda for boards.
why: Board-level AI banking governance essay; position paper

title: AI Risk Mitigation in Finance: Resource Allocation Under Uncertainty and Information Quality
abstract: This study develops a decision framework for allocating limiting resources to AI risk mitigation in financial institutions when risk data are heterogeneous, incomplete, and measured on different scales. It compares four allocation models incorporating historical risk burden, expert-implied mitigation benefits, finance-specific vulnerability, and institutional responsibility. The results show that integrating multiple dimensions can improve allocation stability under varying levels of mitigation-benefit uncertainty and information quality. The integrated models also exhibit relative stability under alternative diminishing-returns parameters and when expert-implied benefits are replaced with a coarser coverage-gap proxy. This framework translates heterogeneous evidence into transparent, reproducible, and comparable decision support for AI risk mitigation.
why: Resource allocation framework for AI risk; no empirical test

title: Publish or Earn? Faculty AI Twins, Compensation Contracts, and the Public Stock of Knowledge
abstract: Business schools have started selling AI twins of their professors: chatbots that talk with students or executives using what a professor knows, at any hour, at any scale. Meanwhile, free tools like ChatGPT learn from everything a professor publishes, then hand it out at no charge. Every idea now poses a choice for the professor: publish it, which feeds the free tools, or keep it for the twin that the school sells. We ask how the way a school pays a professor for the twin, per user or per conversation, shapes that choice.
