Either payment leads professors to keep practical knowledge private while publishing more theory, so the public record of management knowledge becomes more abstract. A simple rule keeps the professor aligned with the school: give the professor the same share of the twin's profit, after computing costs, as of a paper's career value. Sharing revenue instead gets this wrong; rankings that reward practical impact call for an added bonus. Three decisions will therefore determine how much useful knowledge remains public: how employers pay the experts whose knowledge feeds their AI products, how rankings count applied work, whether AI tools credit the sources they learn from.
why: Theory on faculty AI twins and publishing incentives; no data

title: Extending Myerson's Optimal Auctions to Correlated Bidders via Neural Network Interpolation
abstract: We aim to design revenue-maximizing single-item auctions that are deterministic, strategy-proof, and ex post individually rational --- the quintessential fundamental model for optimal mechanism design. While Myerson's seminal work solved this model for independent bidders, straightforward extensions to correlated settings often result in non-monotonic, and therefore non-strategy-proof allocations. Critically, optimal allocation design for correlated bidders is NP-hard to approximate, rendering theoretical optimality guarantees in this domain computationally intractable. We establish a new standard of empirical rigor for this theoretically hard model by proposing an empirical pipeline. We synthesize neural interpolation of Myerson's greedy allocation based on marginal profits (the correlated variant of virtual valuation), formal neural verification to enforce exact strategy-proofness, and a constructive repair procedure. Empirically, our method is highly effective, consistently achieves near-optimal revenue across a wide range of distributions, including synthetic, adversarial, and real-world (consumer, financial, and industrial) datasets. Compared to existing manual and neural baselines, our approach shows substantial improvement, often reducing the revenue gap by an order of magnitude. Our study is also the first to introduce (unattainable) greedy revenue as a rigorous upper bound for empirical benchmarking, providing a definitive quantitative performance measure where true optima remain theoretically elusive. We demonstrate the generality of our approach by extending it to multi-unit auctions with unit demand and integrating our verification techniques into RegretNet to achieve exact strategy-proofness.
why: Neural auction design; not finance, theory-heavy

title: A decomposition-integration framework coupling singular spectrum analysis with a volatility-adaptive LSTM for stock price forecasting
abstract: Financial time series exhibit multi-scale, high-noise, and non-stationary volatility dynamics. Decomposition--integration frameworks built on complete ensemble empirical mode decomposition with adaptive noise (CEEMDAN) have advanced this field, yet existing CEEMDAN hybrids remain unstable: high-frequency mode mixing contaminates downstream predictors, and the heterogeneous volatility of decomposed components is not matched by any volatility-adaptive mechanism. To address these gaps, this paper proposes CEEMDAN-SE-SSA-VMGL. CEEMDAN adaptively decomposes the original series, and sample-entropy-driven K-means clustering groups the intrinsic mode functions into high-, mid-, and low-frequency and residual components. Singular spectrum analysis (SSA) is then applied to the high-frequency group, whose singular-value decomposition of the trajectory matrix and principal-component reconstruction decouple intertwined pseudo-oscillatory modes and alleviate mode mixing. We further design a plug-and-play robust LSTM variant, the volatility-modulated GARCH-LSTM (VMGL), which embeds a differentiable GARCH(1,1) layer inside the LSTM cell as a risk gate; the estimated conditional volatility multiplicatively scales the forget-gate activation, letting memory decay adapt to the instantaneous volatility while remaining fully end-to-end trainable. Component predictions are linearly combined. On five US and Chinese financial series (CSI 300, CSI 500, AAPL, GOOGL, S&P 500), the proposed model is compared with eleven benchmark architectures, lowering the forecasting error by 9% to 24% relative to the best benchmark and by 60% to 70% relative to a standard LSTM. Diebold--Mariano and model-confidence-set (MCS) tests confirm the statistical significance and stability of the gains, spectral analyses verify the SSA denoising efficacy, and backtesting demonstrates the framework's economic utility.
why: CEEMDAN-SSA-LSTM price forecaster; no costs or OOS discipline visible

title: A Symmetry-Matching Approach to Blind-Spot Reduction in Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Language models can treat semantically distinct inputs as interchangeable at the representation level, creating blind spots that standard sparse autoencoder (SAE) objectives do not target. In safety-critical settings such as clinical dosage extraction, legal clause interpretation, or financial amount verification, such failures can propagate silently into downstream decisions. We study this problem as one of feature-basis orientation. Building on a symmetry-matching view from algebraic error-detection theory, we add a differentiable $V_{\mathrm{Gini}}$ regularisation term to SAE training that penalises uneven perturbation response within a specified family. Across GPT-2, Gemma 2, and Qwen 2.5, a frozen multi-seed evaluation shows that $V$-regularisation raises both relative and absolute lower-tail responses while reducing response-profile imbalance, with no material general-text reconstruction degradation. JumpReLU and minimum description length (MDL) objectives remain close to the Standard SAE profile under the same protocol. Family-geometry controls show that the effect is not explained by template duplication or a single dominant perturbation family, and held-out probes plus null-calibrated separation tests evaluate how far the representation-level change carries to downstream discriminability. A zero-shot audit on out-of-distribution clinical radiology minimal pairs finds the relative weak-tail lift in all evaluated model-by-family cells, not perfectly rank-aligned with the trained statistic, and a held-out family audit finds it on family kinds never used in training. Together, the results show that perturbation-aware SAE training can reorient feature bases toward safety-relevant input changes while leaving downstream validation as a separate empirical step.
why: Sparse autoencoder regularisation; finance only mentioned as motivation

title: BrandEval: A Two-Track Multi-Agent Benchmark for Risk-Sensitive LLM Crisis Communication
abstract: Evaluating LLMs for crisis communication requires more than judging isolated responses, because public feedback and competitor actions can reshape trust over time. Existing benchmarks remain largely static and single-turn, offering limited evidence about long-horizon risk-sensitive communication. We introduce \textbf{BrandEval}, a two-track benchmark for product-crisis communication, focusing on public brand responses to product-related safety, quality, service, and trust incidents. BrandEval-Static evaluates stakeholder-aware strategic analysis, while BrandEval-Dynamic stress-tests response policies in \textbf{BrandPolis}, a controlled multi-agent sandbox with consumer feedback, competitor responses, and trust-risk trajectories. We also construct \textbf{BrandSRD}, a Chinese crisis-response dataset, and instantiate a reference Strategic Agent using \textbf{Strategic Rationale (SR)}. Across proprietary and open-source models, we find that static strategic quality is informative but incomplete: it aligns with some end-state outcomes but does not reliably predict volatility and delayed recovery; dynamic stress tests further expose tail-risk failures under manipulative or weakly grounded policies. The code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/htgan-ai/BrandEval.
why: Crisis communication LLM benchmark; not financial work

title: A Calibrated Instrument for Detecting Disposition Drift in Language Models
abstract: Before language models are released, they are tested for harmful traits such as willingness to carry out dangerous requests, deception, power seeking, and sycophancy. The safe behavior these tests certify may degrade as models are modified, by topical fine-tuning, new training data, or changes to settings such as the depth of their reasoning. Most work reports such drift as single summary rates scored by another AI model, without the error analysis needed to interpret them. We adapt a calibrated measurement methodology recently developed for assessing how inference optimizations affect the quality of model outputs. Applying it to several misalignment dimensions in two open-weight models, we first establish the instrument's precision, showing that shifts of a few percentage points can be reliably detected. We then induce drift deliberately by fine-tuning on correct and on subtly harmful medical and financial advice; harmful advice induces a far greater shift than correct advice. Most strikingly, a model that reasons before answering can conceal the shift almost entirely in its answers, even though a direct reading of its internal state shows that its disposition has moved. With reasoning switched off, the same model shifts steadily as the share of harmful advice in its training grows. These results demonstrate the importance of testing safety with reasoning turned both on and off.
why: Model safety drift instrument; not finance

title: Typed Decision Models under Prevalence Shift: Decision Training, Calibration, and Implicit Priors
abstract: Typed decision models (TDMs) return a probability over caller-defined options, and Jev is described by its vendor as calibrated. But in deployment class frequencies change, so calibration measured on a fixed test set need not hold where thresholds are applied. Existing evaluations leave two gaps: the gains of vendor decision training have not been separated from those of the backbone under an identical readout, and TDMs have been tested only at the test set's class distribution. We ask whether decision training improves a model over its own backbone, and whether a TDM's calibration and thresholds withstand prevalence (label) shift as well as a fine-tuned classifier's. We compare three TDMs (Jev, Tev1-4B, Nimble-9B), their base models and two trained classifiers on identical decisions from five public datasets under simulated shift, with 35 paired tests fixed before any test was computed. First, decision training is not uniformly beneficial: Nimble-9B, which differs from Qwen3.5-9B only by a LoRA adapter, is better calibrated on intent tasks but 12.0 Macro-F1 points worse on financial sentiment. Second, under moderate shift Jev's expected calibration error (ECE) and threshold risk grow significantly more than a fine-tuned DeBERTa's only on financial sentiment, by 1.7 and 2.5 percentage points; averaged over 2,000 shift scenarios (exploratory), the gap is at most one point on every dataset. Third, EM prior correction with the model's mean development prediction as its prior needs no labels and lowers Jev's ECE under shift by 2.7 and 1.8 points on the two datasets where it is highest, although labelled recalibration lowers it far more. The three TDMs we tested are neither uniformly better than their backbones nor uniquely fragile under shift; for calibration, their main weakness is the miscalibration they already have without shift. We release all inputs, code and outputs.
why: Typed decision model calibration under prevalence shift; not finance-specific.

title: SHADE: Shrinkage via Halted Alpha-stable Denoising for Heavy-Tailed Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
abstract: Time-series observations are particularly susceptible to noise, and many real-world series have low signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) together with heavy-tailed and time-varying disturbances. When Gaussian diffusion models are used for forecasting, reversing all the way to the zero-noise endpoint may yield an overly narrow and overconfident predictive distribution. We propose SHADE, an alpha-stable Lévy diffusion forecaster that reads out at a nonzero depth so that the residual stable kernel acts as distribution-level shrinkage. By decomposing halting risk into smoothing bias and estimation error, we develop a scale-calibrated halt for estimating the optimal shrinkage $τ^*$ and a context-amortized halt that requires no explicit noise labels. Gains concentrate in the extreme heavy-tailed regime $α\leq1.3$: Across synthetic noise settings, median CRPS improves by 21.7\%, while the NLL falls significantly; Cryptocurrency and foreign-exchange data provide further evidence of improved tail calibration in real-data implement. On near-light-tailed or high-SNR data, the model reverts to Gaussian diffusion or full denoising. SHADE maintains overall forecast error comparable to strong baselines while providing more honest tail uncertainty for heavy-tailed series.
why: Diffusion forecaster for heavy tails; general time series

title: Toward Structured Financial Foundation Models
abstract: Foundation models promise reusable capabilities and step-change performance gains across tasks. In finance, large-scale pretraining of domain-specialized foundation models can advance both goals. However, prevailing architectures and objectives do not by themselves address the combined demands of financial systems: partial observability, interacting entities, asynchronous events, changing regimes, action-dependent outcomes, and rare states with disproportionate consequences. Moreover, independently developed specialists may learn incompatible representations, while multi-domain monolithic alternatives couple data access, model updates, and governance. We therefore propose a structured-data-first research agenda centered on modular, domain-specialized financial foundation models connected by a representation fabric for reuse and composition across domains and tasks. These models should maintain persistent financial state across aggregation levels and time horizons, capture its dynamics, and simulate action-conditioned futures, while remaining calibrated across regimes and for tail outcomes. They must also learn efficiently under data and access constraints and provide faithful, traceable explanations. We identify research challenges, directions, and capability-oriented evaluation criteria.
why: Research agenda for financial foundation models; position paper

title: Probability-Weighting Functions for Normal Tempered-Stable Laws: Orthogonal Channels and Information-Theoretic Indices
abstract: A probability-weighting function (PWF) maps objective probabilities into decision weights. We construct PWFs from changes in the distribution of returns rather than from a parametric family: with prior and posterior return distributions $F_{prior}$ and $F_{post}$, the PWF is $w(p) = F_{post}(F_{prior}^{-1}(p))$. Both distributions are normal tempered-stable (NTS), and the posterior differs from the prior along one of three channels, each isolated with the variance held fixed: scale, skewness and tail thickness. Around a symmetric benchmark with excess kurtosis 3, a 40% change in scale moves cumulative probabilities by up to 7 to 8 percentage points, a skewness of $\pm 0.5$ by 2 percentage points, and a change of $\pm 0.3$ in the tail index by about 2 percentage points. The three channels leave distinct signatures: the deviation $w(p) - p$ changes sign once, twice and three times, respectively. Three information-theoretic indices (a Fisher-normalized logit shift, a signed Jensen-Shannon divergence and a log-odds elasticity) summarize the distortions and avoid the endpoint singularity of the classical ratio $(w(p)-p)/[p(1-p)]$. Applied to NTS parameters calibrated to S&P 500 ETF daily returns over 2015-2025, the same channels produce distortions of 2 to 7 percentage points. Code that reproduces every figure and number in the paper is provided.
why: Probability weighting from NTS distributions; theory without data

title: Game of Phones: Harnessing Game Theory and LLMs in 'Bot Wars' to Counteract Phone Scams
abstract: Phone scams impose substantial and growing costs on individuals and financial systems worldwide, yet existing countermeasures impose no resource cost on perpetrators. Strategic scam-baiting, in which automated agents engage scammers to deplete their operational capacity, offers a proactive alternative but requires dynamic strategy adaptation that static systems cannot provide. We introduce a game-theoretic framework enabling LLMs to learn effective counter-strategies through in-context experience without fine-tuning. The framework models scammer-baiter interactions as a two-player game with empirically grounded strategies and utility functions, using Nash equilibrium as a formal benchmark for evaluating learned behaviour. Across 300 simulated dialogues and three LLM architectures, adaptive strategy selection achieves 28.9-79.7% closer alignment to Nash equilibrium than non-adaptive baselines. The code and an annotated dataset of 300 dialogues with turn-level strategy labels and utility scores are released at https://github.com/nardinebasta/GameofPhones_/ .
why: Game-theoretic scam baiting with LLMs; not finance markets

title: Teacher Supervision, Fixed Representations and Calibration: Exact Risk Calculations for Candidate-Scoring Decision Models
abstract: Candidate-scoring decision models return a probability distribution over a presented set of answers. Public documentation of one such system, Jev, and of an open counterpart, JevAny, describes three training ingredients that determine what these probabilities estimate: soft targets from larger models, a frozen pretrained backbone and temperature calibration. We analyze each ingredient in Gaussian surrogates where the finite-sample risk can be computed exactly. A student trained on teacher targets inherits the teacher's bias, which more student data does not remove and agreement with the teacher does not reveal. A fixed representation lowers the risk only below an explicit sample-size threshold. In a probit model the exact recalibration map is a temperature scaling, which removes all excess risk only when the teacher's coefficient has the correct direction and otherwise leaves a residual that calibration diagnostics do not detect. Under Luce's choice axiom, candidate scores are coherent across refinements of an event if and only if they aggregate by log-sum-exp. On 231,521 credit card complaints from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, where the decision is whether a complaint ends in monetary relief, a student trained on a logistic teacher's probabilities ends at the teacher's decision cost while a student trained on outcomes goes 8% below it, a 30B model read zero-shot remains worse than the teacher after recalibration, and that model departs from the coherence condition by 17.5 decibans. Pretrained representations reduce the labeled data required and calibration corrects the scale of the probabilities, but neither corrects a biased teacher, so the probabilities have to be checked against realized outcomes.
why: Exact risk calculations for candidate-scoring models; theory only

title: A Conceptual Framework on AI-Cybersecurity Capital: An Extended Review
abstract: This review extends Bourdieusian capital theory into a domain that has not yet been addressed in forms of literature: the convergence of artificial intelligence fluency and cybersecurity competence. Building on Archer et al.'s (2015) conceptualization of "science capital" as a magnifier for understanding unbalanced participation in science and on subsequent work extending Bourdieu's framework into digital contexts (Ragnedda, 2018; Verwiebe & Hagemann, 2024), this review argues that AI fluency and cybersecurity competence have become practically inseparable and should be hypothesized together as a single cohesive form of capital rather than as adjacent or embedded structures. Drawing on technical standards such as OWASP, NIST, MITRE ATLAS; regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act; and current workforce data, the review documents the entanglement of AI systems with both offensive and defensive cybersecurity practice. It applies Verwiebe and Hagemann's two-part test for capital independence requires the capital to circulate across subfields and have an unequal, class-structured distribution to argue that this entanglement qualifies as a distinct form of capital. The review builds a new framework called AI-Cybersecurity Capital by combining Archer et al.'s eight dimensions of science capital with Dakan and Feller's (2025) four-part AI fluency model, which provides the structural organization, and maps the result onto three subfields: dispositional and cognitive, behavioral, and relational. The review directly engages Ben Fine's (2001, 2010) warning about inventing too many types of "capital," and maintains that this new concept may be necessary because of structural changes within the industry rather than convenience or theory for its own sake. The model requires empirical data to be fully validated.
why: Conceptual review on AI-cybersecurity capital; no finance content

title: As the Market Grows: Balancing Profits with Regulatory Readiness for Effective AI Adoption within Nigeria's Health Sector
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is creating significant investment opportunities within Nigeria's healthcare sector, promising improvements in diagnosis, clinical decision-making, and healthcare delivery. However, as the market expands, questions surrounding patient safety, algorithmic bias, data integrity, explainability, and legal accountability become increasingly urgent. This paper examines whether Nigeria's existing legal and institutional frameworks are adequately prepared to govern the risks associated with AI adoption in healthcare. It critically evaluates the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999 (as amended), the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, the National Health Act 2014, and other relevant medical, consumer protection, and technology regulation instruments. The paper identifies significant gaps in the regulation of AI-enabled medical technologies, particularly regarding clinical validation, liability allocation, algorithmic accountability, and effective redress for patients harmed by AI-assisted decisions. It further examines emerging policy responses, including Nigeria's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, to assess the country's readiness for responsible AI adoption. The paper argues that regulatory uncertainty, if left unaddressed, could undermine patient protection and create opportunities for regulatory arbitrage as commercial investment accelerates. It therefore advocates a proactive, risk-based regulatory approach that aligns market growth with enforceable safeguards, institutional coordination, and clear accountability mechanisms. Ultimately, Nigeria's ability to realise the benefits of AI in healthcare will depend not merely on its capacity to attract investment and deploy innovative technologies, but also on its ability to ensure that innovation remains safe, equitable, and accountable.
why: Nigerian health regulation policy review; off-topic

title: (Pay)check Please. Staff Auditor Apathy in PE-Backed Accounting Firms
abstract: Private equity (PE) investment is transforming the structure and operations of public accounting firms, yet its effects on early-career professionals remain largely unexplored. We examine how PE investment affects staff auditors’ workplace experiences using a mixed-methods approach combining archival and interview data. Our archival analysis indicates that, relative to staff at non-PE-backed firms, staff at PE-backed firms work fewer hours following PE investment, while compensation and overall job satisfaction remain unchanged. The data further indicate declining perceptions of career opportunities, organizational culture, and senior management. To understand these findings, we interview 17 staff auditors at PE-backed firms. Our qualitative analysis reveals a broader sense of apathy stemming from perceptions of declining organizational commitment, diminished professional development, cultural change, and uncertainty surrounding career progression. Staff particularly view increased reliance on artificial intelligence, offshoring, cost cutting, and changes to the partnership model as reducing the long-term value of careers in public accounting.
why: Qualitative study of PE-backed auditing staff; no ML or markets.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Labour Replacement in Greater Manchester Occupational Exposure, the Augmentation-Substitution Frontier and the AI Pricing Problem
abstract: This interim paper assesses AI labour replacement risk across Greater Manchester's ten boroughs. It applies AI occupational and industry exposure indices to Census 2021 and Companies House data, with LLM-assisted estimates of whether AI will mainly augment or replace work in each sector and a place-based adjustment for ecosystem density. Most of the city-region's workforce sits in the augmentation zone, but only just above the substitution threshold, and exposure varies between and within boroughs. Among firms with four or more employees, boroughs with higher AI exposure show lower augmentation probabilities, the reverse of the UK-wide pattern and consistent with Bessen's account of technology eventually reducing labour demand. Microbusinesses follow the national pattern. Vendors' moves towards cost-recovery pricing add a further risk for organisations dependent on subsidised AI. The paper makes eleven recommendations, centred on pricing resilience, borough-level policy, early-career pipelines, and extending AI to occupations where it is most likely to augment workers.
why: Greater Manchester labour exposure study; no finance ML content.

title: Digital-twin-enabled interpretable machine learning for the building-stock carbon balance of cities: A Stock-Flow-Sink-Response framework with multi-city experiments
abstract: Cities host the majority of building-sector greenhouse-gas emissions, yet urban carbon accounting rarely integrates the physical building stock, the material and energy flows it mobilises, the biogenic and material sinks it can accommodate, and the policy responses that reshape them. This study introduces a Stock-Flow-Sink-Response (SFSR) framework and a computable Building-Stock Carbon Balance (BSCB) identity, BSCB = Sink - (embodied + operational), operationalised through a building-scale digital twin (BIM, GIS and smart-meter Internet of Things) coupled with city-scale dynamic material-flow analysis. A balanced panel of 36 Chinese cities spanning all five climate zones and four functional types was reconstructed for 2015-2024. An engineering-anchor plus LightGBM residual hybrid, explained with SHapley Additive exPlanations, was benchmarked against nine alternatives; partial least squares structural equation modelling decomposed direct and mediated paths, and Monte Carlo simulation evaluated five mitigation scenarios. The BSCB remained negative throughout, narrowing from -581.50 to -460.38 Mt CO2, a roughly 21% deficit reduction. The hybrid reached R2 = 0.946 under cross-validation and 0.945 on a temporal hold-out, where pure gradient-boosted trees collapsed (R2 = -0.097). SHAP identified marginal-effect thresholds for low-carbon materials (about 0.15), cumulative retrofit (about 0.20) and on-site renewables (about 0.08). No embodied-operational crossover occurred under business-as-usual; only the combined scenario achieved it with probability 1.00 near 2034. Urban green sinks contributed below 3% of gross emissions and cannot close the deficit.
why: Building carbon accounting digital twin; off-topic

title: A Pricing and Hedging Framework for Infinite-Dimensional Financial Markets
abstract: In this paper, we provide a comprehensive study of how the classical Black--Scholes-type market framework behaves in an infinite-dimensional setting. The asset prices are modeled by stochastic evolution equations in a separable Hilbert space. The evolution of the risk-free asset and the corresponding discounting operators are governed by a strongly continuous group of bounded linear operators. Accordingly, we consider contingent claims with Hilbert-space-valued payoffs, whose values are discounted through the corresponding operators. Within this framework, we investigate the pricing and hedging of contingent claims, deriving the corresponding infinite-dimensional Black--Scholes equations and establishing exact replication results for strong solutions and asymptotic replication results for mild solutions through Yosida approximations. We also study the special case where the infinitesimal generator is given by $A=rI$, allowing for real-valued contingent claims. We further investigate no-arbitrage and market completeness, introducing a Hilbert lattice structure to formulate arbitrage and characterizing attainability through operator equations associated with martingale representations. Finite-dimensional noise truncations and Yosida approximations are employed to establish approximate and asymptotic approximate completeness results. We introduce geometric Brownian motions in Hilbert spaces and derive sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of an equivalent risk-neutral measure, together with explicit pricing formulas for some tractable examples. These results extend key aspects of the classical Black--Scholes framework to markets with infinite-dimensional asset-price dynamics. As a concrete application, the model can be interpreted as a segmented market consisting of a sequence of one-dimensional geometric Brownian motions.
why: Infinite-dimensional Black-Scholes theory; pure math without implementation path.

title: MELD: Recursive Self-Improvement via Hierarchical Coordination for Multi-Agent Scientific Discovery
abstract: Multi-agent scientific discovery with large language models raises a coupled learning problem: research assignments determine both which experiments are pursued and the experiences from which agents adapt. We introduce MELD, a unified hierarchical test-time training framework that jointly adapts a team-level Coordinator policy and agent-level individual Scientist policies within a single discovery process. The Coordinator generates a joint portfolio of search branches and research directives over a shared derivation tree, while Scientists develop hypotheses and execution plans implemented by a shared frozen Executor. Both levels receive alternating GRPO-style parameter updates under a shared smooth best-of-budget objective, allowing team organization and individual research behavior to co-evolve in a recursive self-improvement loop. Our analysis establishes objective alignment for the hierarchy, characterizes conditions for coordination gains over independent parallel discovery and the first-order benefit of private adaptation, and derives a finite-budget regret bound for adapted models. On 22 MLGym and MLE-bench tasks, MELD is best on 20 of them and achieves the highest aggregate normalized scores on MLGym, using a 4B backbone for coordination and research. Most baselines use proprietary Scientists, and all systems share one frozen Executor.
why: Multi-agent scientific discovery training; not finance

title: HABIT-Bench: Evaluating Habit Induction from Longitudinal Weak Evidence in Agent Memory
abstract: In long-term interactions with large language model (LLM) agents, users reveal habits through their choices and actions. These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations. However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about a habit or when it applies. Retaining past interactions alone does not ensure that agents can infer habits and apply them appropriately. We introduce HABIT-Bench to evaluate how well agent memory systems infer habits from weak evidence and apply them to later requests. We construct synthetic user histories from task-oriented dialogue data and controlled habit graphs. The histories span hundreds of sessions across food, finance, software, and travel. Four-choice tasks assess agents' ability to infer user habits and apply them appropriately. They include temporary exceptions, changes in habits, and suggestions that users have not accepted. Sampled tasks undergo independent human review. We evaluate eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash. The best-performing memory method achieves 33.61\% macro accuracy across the four domains. Performance remains limited even when annotated evidence is supplied directly. These results expose a persistent gap between access to past interactions and the ability to infer and appropriately use user habits.
why: Agent memory benchmark for habits; finance only incidental.

title: Mining the Self-Rewriting System: A Vision for Data Mining on AI-Native Infrastructure
abstract: Classical data mining treats data as generated outside the learner. Emerging AI-native infrastructure invalidates this assumption: as agents observe system state, act, update retrieval stores and models, and promote new artifacts into the serving path, their own decisions reshape the future logs, traces, corpora, and evaluation records used for later training and release. We call this new research object a self-rewriting system and the resulting system-induced distribution shift endogenous drift. Our central, falsifiable claim is that cross-surface causes are not identifiable in general from marginal per-surface monitoring: different coupled failures can produce the same individual signals while differing in their joint behavior, requiring joint analysis for reliable attribution. This agenda comprises four foundational research problems: fusing heterogeneous drift signals into calibrated gating and attribution (C1); mining agent traces whose activity alphabet evolves (C2); maintaining knowledge fabrics through online reindexing, faithfulness, and compression decisions (C3); and safely promoting concurrent learning streams through one shared evaluation gate (C4). These remain fragmented across concept drift, performative prediction, process mining, streaming retrieval-augmented generation, and MLOps, without a unified data-mining agenda. We outline public benchmarks and evaluation criteria, using AI-native telecom only as a motivating exemplar with analogues in finance, software CI/CD, and clinical decision support.
why: Vision paper on self-rewriting systems; no finance

title: StopLoss: Teaching Agents to Predict Failure and Stop Early
abstract: Coding agents keep working on runs that will fail verification, and asking a frontier model to watch for this is expensive in its own right. We introduce StopLoss, a small external monitor that learns failure recognition from completed trajectories and their verifier outcomes. The name is inspired by the stop-loss order in finance: StopLoss ends a run early when the run is likely to fail, which saves resources. Final outcomes label earlier local windows, so a fine-tuned language model can score the most recent tool steps in a single forward pass, and a threshold calibrated on successful runs turns that score into an abort decision without changing the executor. Trained on GPT-family SWE-rebench trajectories and evaluated on SWE-bench Verified and a SWE-bench Pro subset with GPT and Claude executors, StopLoss is compared against six general-purpose judges reading identical windows. Outcome supervision lifts failure prediction from near chance to a useful signal at the first check, at one to two orders of magnitude lower cost per check than any tested judge. This translates into savings: relative to completing every task, StopLoss lowers cost per retained solve by 4.5\% on Verified while preserving 99\% of successful runs, and by up to 31\% on the costlier Pro subset, reaching 48\% with a Qwen3-8B backbone, and in all four settings its cost per retained solve is below that of every judge policy. Outcome-trained small monitors can make failure recognition cheap enough for early stopping to pay for itself.
why: Coding-agent early stopping; stop-loss analogy only, not finance.

title: StrucChunk: Structure-Aware Retrieval for Legal Document RAG
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can ground LLM outputs in domain-specific knowledge, but legal documents are hard: standard chunking fragments hierarchical argument structure, and generic embeddings struggle with both precise citation matching and semantic understanding. We propose StrucChunk (Structure Aware Chunking) with hybrid dense-sparse retrieval for hierarchically structured legal documents. It treats documents as directed acyclic graphs of provisions, preserves clause boundaries, resolves cross-references before embedding, and combines BM25 with BGE-M3 via Reciprocal Rank Fusion. We evaluate on five corpora, three legal traditions and two languages. StrucChunk reaches 100% boundary precision (vs. 7.7% for recursive splitting on CrPC), preserves 97.6% of documented cross-references (vs. 0%), and matches section coverage with 40.3% fewer chunks on GDPR. On LegalBench-RAG (6,858 query-passage pairs), it achieves Char-Recall@8 of 48.18% vs. 23.59% for the best baseline (+104%), surpassing the published state of the art by +83%. On 501 queries each for CrPC and CPC (Indian law), Recall@5 improves from 0.557 to 0.804 (+44.4%) and from 0.158 to 0.259 (+64.6%); chunking accounts for 88% and 73% of the gain. On 501 GDPR queries, Recall@5 is 0.868 with R@1 improving +59%. On NitiBench-CCL (3,730 Thai financial law queries), HR@5 is 0.856 vs. 0.594 for naive chunking (+44.1%), showing that section-boundary alignment is the dominant factor across languages, and cross-reference augmentation adds +2.3% on cross-reference queries. We release the implementation, 5,256 evaluation queries across five legal corpora, annotation methodology and chunking quality metrics. Code: github.com/SinghSuryaDeep/legal-rag-strucchunk-1
why: Legal document RAG; not finance

title: Injection of Space Radiation Errors on Low-power NVM using Generative Deep Learning
abstract: We develop an error model for a Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) device that represents the effects of physical faults experienced in a CubeSat mission in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). The CubeSat carries an off-the-shelf low-power Ferroelectric RAM (FRAM) chip and runs repeated read/write tests according to a predefined pattern. We compare every memory snapshot received from the satellite with a reference bitmap to identify bit errors. We visually analyze erroneous values distributions in the memory snapshots and we understand that they are frequently distributed according to regular spatial patterns. We define a generative deep learning technique to automatically learn these spatial patterns and to synthetically generate additional error patterns mimicking the observed ones. The model is capable at producing memory errors for general application-level experimentation. Our preliminary validation indicates that when comparing the model output with the data we collect, 0.92 of the generated bit flips correspond to bit flips in the memory snapshots and the model captures 0.91 of the observed bit flips.
